secondaryCondition: Myositis (statin-associated immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy with anti-HMGCR autoantibodies) in a veteran on statin therapy for service-connected hypertension
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5021 (myositis) — with the note to DCs 5013 through 5024 directing that group to be evaluated as degenerative arthritis based on limitation of motion; where the predominant disability is proximal muscle weakness and fatigue rather than joint limitation, the muscle-injury provisions of § 4.73 and the evaluation of muscle disability in § 4.56 govern, and an analogous evaluation under §§ 4.20 and 4.27 may be required. Qualified-human rating review required
primaryCondition: Service-connected hypertensive vascular disease (hypertension) for which a statin was prescribed as part of cardiovascular risk management
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.104, DC 7101 (hypertensive vascular disease (hypertension and isolated systolic hypertension)): 10/20/40/60 percent on diastolic or systolic pressure thresholds, or as the minimum evaluation for a history of diastolic pressure predominantly 100 or more requiring continuous medication for control, with Note (1) requiring confirmation by readings taken two or more times on at least three different days
etiologicalMechanism: Pharmacological iatrogenic sequence: statins inhibit 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis. In genetically susceptible patients the drug upregulates expression of the HMGCR protein in regenerating skeletal muscle, and that overexpressed enzyme becomes the target of a specific autoantibody response, producing an immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy characterized by symmetric proximal muscle weakness, markedly elevated creatine kinase, myofiber necrosis with minimal inflammation on biopsy, and — critically — persistence and even progression after the statin is withdrawn, which distinguishes it from the self-limited toxic myopathy that resolves on discontinuation. Because the disease is antibody-driven rather than simply dose-toxic, the ordinary temporal assumption that stopping the drug ends the illness does not hold. Mammen et al. (PMID 21360500) identified anti-HMGCR autoantibodies in 45 of 750 patients presenting to a myositis center, with the great majority of patients aged 50 and older having had statin exposure, and demonstrated the statin-dependent upregulation of the autoantigen. Nazir et al. (PMID 28277343) systematically reviewed 100 reported cases of statin-associated autoimmune myopathy and described a syndrome of symmetric proximal weakness with extreme creatine kinase elevation, occurring predominantly in males, and separate from the ordinary statin myalgia that resolves on drug cessation. Khoo et al. (PMID 40347460) calculated the incidence of anti-HMGCR immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy across four independent cohorts in the United Kingdom and Australia and described its clinical characteristics, treating it as a rare but definable complication of statin therapy — the contemporary denominator evidence for a rare-event claim. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) proximate-causation theory pleaded as a medication side effect, in which a disability caused by treatment of the service-connected hypertension is itself service-connected because the statin was prescribed for that service-connected condition. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; aggravation would be the correct theory only where the record documents pre-existing myositis, inflammatory myopathy, or another myopathic process and the claim is that the statin exposure measurably worsened that baseline muscle disease, in which case the drug-attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of the pre-existing myopathy and § 3.310(b) governs. Chronology and the individual analysis under § 3.310(a) or (b) require: a prescription record identifying the statin with start and stop dates and the indication of the service-connected hypertension or its cardiovascular risk profile; onset of proximal weakness during or after exposure; laboratory confirmation of markedly elevated creatine kinase; and, where available, positive anti-HMGCR antibody testing or muscle biopsy showing necrotizing myopathy, since the antibody and biopsy findings are what distinguish the immune-mediated disease from ordinary statin myalgia. Only then can an examiner state that the myositis is at least as likely as not caused by the statin prescribed for the service-connected hypertension — a conclusion requiring documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include ordinary statin-associated myalgia and self-limited toxic myopathy, hypothyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, inflammatory myopathies unrelated to statins (dermatomyositis, polymyositis, and other immune-mediated necrotizing myopathies), paraneoplastic myositis associated with an occult malignancy, viral myositis including influenza, HIV, and hepatitis, glucocorticoid or colchicine myopathy, alcohol-related muscle disease, and inherited metabolic myopathies. No individual probability is asserted here. No intentional rechallenge, unsupervised discontinuation of a prescribed statin, or patient-specific prescribing recommendation is made. Rating discipline under § 4.14: the same weakness, creatine kinase elevation, or limitation of motion may not be compensated more than once — a myositis rating under DC 5021 and a separate muscle-injury rating for the same proximal groups are not cumulative, and § 4.14 and the note to DCs 5013 through 5024 require a single evaluation for the same manifestation.

secondaryCondition: Tarsal tunnel syndrome (posterior tibial nerve entrapment at the ankle with plantar burning, numbness and neuropathic pain) in a veteran with service-connected type 2 diabetes mellitus
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.124a, DC 8525 (posterior tibial nerve): 30 percent complete, 20 percent severe incomplete, 10 percent moderate, 10 percent mild, with DC 8625 (neuritis) as the alternative code for a predominantly inflammatory-painful presentation and DC 8725 (neuralgia) for a purely sensory pain presentation; DC 8524 (internal popliteal nerve (tibial)) is the proximal comparator where the lesion is above the tarsal tunnel. Qualified-human rating review required
primaryCondition: Service-connected type 2 diabetes mellitus with documented duration and glycemic history
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.119, DC 7913 (diabetes mellitus), assigned on the insulin, dietary, activity-regulation and complication tiers, with the note to DC 7913 addressing the relationship between diabetes and its separately evaluated complications
etiologicalMechanism: Metabolic-and-entrapment sequence: in service-connected type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic hyperglycemia produces a diffuse neuropathy through polyol-pathway flux with sorbitol accumulation, advanced glycation end-product formation, oxidative stress, and endoneurial microangiopathy. In the tarsal tunnel those metabolic effects are compounded by two diabetes-related structural changes: glycosylation of connective tissue thickens the flexor retinaculum and the epineurium, narrowing the fibro-osseous tunnel through which the posterior tibial nerve and its plantar branches pass behind the medial malleolus, and the increased body mass that frequently accompanies type 2 diabetes raises the compressive load on that confined space. The combination converts a normal anatomic narrowing into a focal compressive mononeuropathy producing burning pain, numbness, and paresthesias along the medial ankle and plantar surface, with a positive Tinel sign and electrodiagnostic slowing across the tunnel. Rinkel et al. (PMID 30113445), a cross-sectional study in both diabetic and nondiabetic subjects, reported a prevalence of tibial nerve entrapment at the tarsal tunnel of 44.9 percent in diabetic patients versus 26.5 percent in nondiabetic subjects, and assessed the validity of the Tinel sign for the diagnosis. Rinkel et al. (PMID 32276769) then followed the natural history of tarsal tunnel syndrome in diabetic subjects and reported that tibial nerve entrapment is highly prevalent in diabetes, producing significantly more neuropathic complaints and concomitant sensory disturbance, and they studied its relationship to incident diabetic foot ulceration. Omirah et al. (PMID 40591366) examined the association between body mass index, HbA1c level and tarsal tunnel syndrome severity in a clinical and neurophysiological study, treating the condition as a focal compressive entrapment neuropathy of the posterior tibial nerve in which obesity and diabetes are systemic risk factors. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) direct-causation theory — the service-connected diabetes is asserted to have produced a distinct focal entrapment mononeuropathy with its own diagnostic code, not merely a diffuse distal polyneuropathy. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; aggravation would govern only where the record shows pre-existing tarsal tunnel syndrome (for example, from prior ankle fracture, hindfoot deformity, or a space-occupying lesion) and the claim is that the diabetic metabolic and structural changes measurably worsened a baseline entrapment, in which case the diabetic increment must be separated from the natural progression of the pre-existing compression and § 3.310(b) applies. Chronology and the individual analysis under § 3.310(a) or (b) require: a documented diagnosis of type 2 diabetes with its laboratory confirmation and duration; clinical localization of symptoms to the tarsal tunnel; and electrodiagnostic confirmation — nerve conduction studies showing focal slowing or conduction block of the tibial nerve across the tarsal tunnel, ideally with comparison of plantar sensory responses with the unaffected side — rather than reliance on a Tinel sign alone, since the physical sign alone had imperfect validity in the cited study. Only with that evidence can an examiner state that the tarsal tunnel syndrome is at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected diabetes — a conclusion requiring documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include coexisting diabetic distal symmetric polyneuropathy (which is a different, separately rated entity and must not be used twice for the same sensory loss), obesity independent of diabetes, prior ankle fracture or hindfoot deformity, tenosynovitis or ganglion cyst in the tunnel, venous varicosities, hypothyroidism, alcohol-related neuropathy, vitamin B12 deficiency, and lumbosacral radiculopathy producing a similar plantar distribution. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating discipline under § 4.14 and the note to DC 7913: the same sensory deficit in the same distribution may not support both a diabetic polyneuropathy rating and a tarsal tunnel rating on the same extremity, and only one of DC 8525, DC 8625 or DC 8725 may be used for the same nerve.

medicalEvidence.authors: Willem D Rinkel; Manuel Castro Cabezas; Johan W van Neck; Erwin Birnie; Steven E R Hovius; J Henk Coert
medicalEvidence.summary: Cross-sectional study reporting a prevalence of tibial nerve entrapment at the tarsal tunnel of 44.9 percent in diabetic patients versus 26.5 percent in nondiabetic subjects, and evaluating the diagnostic validity of the Tinel sign — the primary comparative prevalence evidence for the diabetes-to-entrapment pathway.

medicalEvidence.title: The natural history of tarsal tunnel syndrome in diabetic subjects

medicalEvidence.summary: Follow-up study reporting that tibial nerve entrapment is highly prevalent in diabetic subjects and results in significantly more neuropathic complaints and concomitant sensory disturbance, and assessing the impact of tarsal tunnel syndrome on incident diabetic foot ulceration — the prognostic evidence that the entrapment is clinically consequential in diabetes.

medicalEvidence.title: The Association between Body Mass Index, HbA1c Levels, and Tarsal Tunnel Syndrome: A Clinical and Neurophysiological Study
medicalEvidence.authors: Marwa Hanafy Abo Omirah; Marwa Kamal; Mohammed Gomaa; Abdelrahman Ahmed Ewais; Hayam Ali AlRasheed; Mostafa M Bahaa; Sherif Thabet; Hossam Mostafa Moawad; Mostafa M Magdy

secondaryCondition: Toxic epidermal necrolysis (drug-induced severe cutaneous adverse reaction with chronic cutaneous, ocular and mucosal sequelae) in a veteran receiving allopurinol for service-connected gout
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.118, DC 7827 (erythema multiforme; toxic epidermal necrolysis): 60 percent for recurrent mucosal, palmar, or plantar involvement impairing mastication, use of hands, or ambulation occurring four or more times over the past 12-month period despite ongoing immunosuppressive therapy; 30 percent for the corresponding recurrent pattern requiring intermittent systemic therapy; 10 percent for one to three such episodes in the past 12-month period or continuous systemic medication for control; alternatively rated as disfigurement of the head, face, or neck (DC 7800) or scars (DCs 7801, 7802, 7804, 7805) depending on the predominant disability. Ocular and other mucosal sequelae are separately rated in the affected system. Qualified-human rating review required
primaryCondition: Service-connected gout for which allopurinol was prescribed
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5017 (gout) — evaluated as degenerative arthritis based on limitation of motion of affected parts under the note to DCs 5013 through 5024
etiologicalMechanism: Pharmacological iatrogenic sequence: allopurinol is metabolized to oxypurinol, and in carriers of the HLA-B*58:01 allele the drug and its metabolite are presented as drug-specific antigens that activate cytotoxic CD8+ T lymphocytes. The activated T cells release granulysin, perforin, and Fas-ligand, which trigger widespread keratinocyte apoptosis and detachment of the full-thickness epidermis — the mechanism of toxic epidermal necrolysis when detachment exceeds 30 percent of body surface area, and of Stevens-Johnson syndrome below that threshold. Mucosal surfaces, including the ocular surface and the oral, genital, and respiratory mucosae, are involved by the same cytotoxic process, and survivors are left with chronic morbidity: hypertrophic and dyspigmented scarring, sicca and ocular surface failure with symblepharon formation, oral and genital mucosal strictures, and recurrent mucosal episodes. Halevy et al. (PMID 17919772), a multinational case-control study, found that allopurinol was the single most common cause of Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis in Europe and Israel and identified risk factors for allopurinol-associated disease — the primary causal attribution evidence for this drug. Somkrua et al. (PMID 21906289) systematically reviewed and meta-analyzed the association between the HLA-B*5801 allele and allopurinol-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis and found a strong and significant association, concluding that allele screening may be considered in populations at risk. Gonçalo et al. (PMID 23600531) studied 25 Portuguese patients with allopurinol-induced severe cutaneous adverse reactions, including DRESS and Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis cases, and confirmed HLA-B*58:01 as a risk factor in a European population, extending the association beyond Han Chinese cohorts. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) proximate-causation theory pleaded as a medication side effect, in which a disability caused by treatment of the service-connected gout is itself service-connected because the allopurinol was prescribed for the service-connected condition; the compensable disability in most cases is the residual scarring, ocular surface disease, and mucosal sequelae rather than the acute hospitalization. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; aggravation would govern only where the record shows a pre-existing skin disease such as psoriasis or another blistering disorder and the claim is that the drug reaction worsened a baseline dermatosis, in which case the drug-attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of the pre-existing disease and § 3.310(b) applies. Chronology and the individual analysis under § 3.310(a) or (b) require: a prescription record identifying allopurinol with start and stop dates and the gout indication; acute-onset mucocutaneous disease documented by dermatology, ideally with histopathology or a registry-classified diagnosis of Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis with the estimated percentage of body surface area detached; the implicated-drug reasoning recorded in the acute admission; and documentation of the chronic sequelae that are actually being rated, such as scar extent, ocular surface findings, or mucosal stricture. Only then can an examiner state that the toxic epidermal necrolysis and its sequelae are at least as likely as not caused by the allopurinol prescribed for the service-connected gout — a conclusion requiring documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include other high-risk culprits that are frequently co-prescribed — aromatic anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine, phenobarbital), sulfonamide antibiotics and sulfasalazine, nevirapine, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs of the oxicam class, and the newer checkpoint inhibitors — as well as DRESS syndrome with a different natural history, staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, pemphigus vulgaris, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, and graft-versus-host disease. A specific causality caution must be disclosed: HLA-B*58:01 carriage is strongly associated with but is neither necessary nor sufficient for allopurinol hypersensitivity in every population, and the cited case-control data are population-level attributions, so a positive genotype or a negative genotype neither proves nor disproves causation in one veteran, and the acute drug-attribution reasoning recorded at the time of illness is the strongest single piece of evidence. No individual probability is asserted here. No intentional rechallenge, unsupervised discontinuation of a prescribed medication, or patient-specific prescribing recommendation is made. Rating discipline under § 4.14 and § 4.118(b): two skin conditions may be combined only where separate areas of skin are involved, and where the same skin supports ratings under DC 7827 and DC 7800, DC 7801 or DC 7804, only the higher single evaluation may be assigned for that area; ocular sequelae rated under § 4.79 are separate disabilities and must not be used twice.

secondaryCondition: Peritoneal adhesions (post-surgical adhesive disease with recurrent or intermittent small bowel obstruction) following open cholecystectomy for service-connected cholelithiasis
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.114, DC 7301 (peritoneum, adhesions of, due to surgery, trauma, disease, or infection): 80 percent for persistent partial bowel obstruction that is inoperable and refractory to treatment or requires total parenteral nutrition; 50 percent for symptomatic adhesions persisting or recurring after surgery with documented dietary modification and clinical evidence of recurrent obstruction requiring hospitalization at least once a year plus at least one of abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, colic, constipation, or diarrhea; 30 percent for the same symptomatic pattern without the hospitalization requirement; 10 percent for symptomatic adhesions with at least one of those symptoms; 0 percent for history of adhesions currently asymptomatic. Qualified-human rating review required
primaryCondition: Service-connected cholelithiasis requiring cholecystectomy, performed as an open procedure
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.114, DC 7315 (cholelithiasis, chronic) rated as DC 7314 (chronic biliary tract disease): 30 percent with three or more clinically documented attacks of right-upper-quadrant pain with nausea and vomiting in the past 12 months or requiring biliary stricture dilatation at least once in the past 12 months; 10 percent with one or two such attacks; 0 percent if asymptomatic without a documented attack; with DC 7318 for complications of cholecystectomy such as strictures and biliary leaks
etiologicalMechanism: Surgical peritoneal-injury sequence: opening the peritoneal cavity causes mesothelial injury, local ischemia at the operative site, and an inflammatory exudate of fibrinogen that is converted to fibrin. When the peritoneal fibrinolytic capacity is overwhelmed — as it is in the days after laparotomy — the fibrinous bridges are not lysed but become organized by fibroblast in-growth and angiogenesis into permanent collagenous adhesions that tether bowel to the abdominal wall, the liver bed, or adjacent viscera. Those bands cause traction, kinking, and mesenteric distortion that can produce intermittent partial obstruction with colicky pain, nausea, vomiting, and constipation, and can progress to complete small bowel obstruction or internal herniation requiring emergency surgery; each subsequent adhesiolysis creates new peritoneal injury and new adhesions, so the process is self-reinforcing. Ellis et al. (PMID 10232313), a retrospective cohort using Scottish National Health Service record-linkage data, found that 34.6 percent of 29,790 patients who underwent open abdominal or pelvic surgery in a single year were readmitted a mean of 2.1 times over 10 years for a disorder that could be directly or possibly linked to adhesions, and that nearly a fifth of those readmissions were directly attributable to adhesions. Tingstedt et al. (PMID 17330836) followed 102 patients operated for adhesion-caused small bowel obstruction with a median follow-up of about 14 years and reported long-term readmission and cost outcomes, finding a higher readmission rate than previously reported. Lorentzen et al. (PMID 29030779) reviewed patients requiring emergency surgery for adhesive small bowel obstruction and found an overall recurrence rate of about 12 percent, with risk persisting for years after the index operation. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) proximate-causation theory, in which a disability resulting from surgery performed to treat the service-connected cholelithiasis is itself proximately due to that service-connected condition, so the cholelithiasis that necessitated the cholecystectomy is the legal and medical predicate for adhesions produced by that operation. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; aggravation would govern only where the record shows pre-existing peritoneal adhesions from earlier abdominal surgery, endometriosis, or intra-abdominal infection and the claim is that the new operation measurably worsened a baseline adhesive burden, in which case the new-surgery increment must be separated from the natural progression of the pre-existing adhesions and § 3.310(b) applies. Chronology and the individual analysis under § 3.310(a) or (b) require: documentation of the service-connected cholelithiasis; the operative note establishing that an open cholecystectomy was performed and describing the peritoneal field; an interval during which obstruction symptoms appear after the operation rather than before it; and objective findings of adhesive obstruction or tethering — imaging showing a transition point, adhesions at reoperation, or operative findings of bands — rather than pain alone. Only then can an examiner state that the peritoneal adhesions are at least as likely as not caused by the open cholecystectomy performed for the service-connected cholelithiasis — a conclusion requiring documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102. Two candid limitations must be disclosed. First, the strength of this theory depends on the surgical approach: laparoscopic cholecystectomy carries a substantially lower adhesion-related readmission risk than open surgery, so a laparoscopic operation weakens but does not automatically defeat the claim, and the operative report is decisive. Second, adhesions are a common incidental finding in any patient who has undergone abdominal surgery, so the nexus opinion must link the specific symptom pattern to documented adhesive obstruction rather than to coexisting conditions. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include other surgical and non-surgical causes of bowel obstruction (hernia, malignancy, Crohn's disease, gallstone ileus, bezoars), irritable bowel syndrome and chronic constipation, gastroparesis, chronic cholecystitis and post-cholecystectomy syndrome, endometriosis, prior surgery in any quadrant, and peritonitis or abscess from the index episode. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating discipline under § 4.14 and the anti-pyramiding instruction of § 4.114: the same abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and constipation may not be compensated simultaneously under the cirrhosis, gastropathy, or post-cholecystectomy codes and again under the adhesion code, and where more than one rating is warranted under DCs 7301 through 7329 the schedule requires a single evaluation reflecting the predominant disability picture.

secondaryCondition: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (stress-induced cardiomyopathy with residual or recurrent left ventricular dysfunction) in a veteran with service-connected post-traumatic stress disorder
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.104, DC 7020 (cardiomyopathy) — evaluated under the General Rating Formula for Diseases of the Heart, which assigns 100 percent when a workload of 3.0 METs or less produces heart failure symptoms, 60 percent at 3.1 to 5.0 METs, 30 percent at 5.1 to 7.0 METs or with echocardiographic evidence of cardiac hypertrophy or dilatation, and 10 percent at 7.1 to 10.0 METs or when continuous medication is required for control. Qualified-human rating review required; because stress cardiomyopathy is typically reversible, a compensable evaluation depends on documented persistent or recurrent ventricular dysfunction rather than on the acute episode alone
primaryCondition: Service-connected post-traumatic stress disorder, with a documented stressor and ongoing symptom severity
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.130, DC 9411 (posttraumatic stress disorder), rated under the General Rating Formula for Mental Disorders at 0, 10, 30, 50, 70, or 100 percent
etiologicalMechanism: Neuroendocrine-to-myocardial sequence: post-traumatic stress disorder is characterized by sustained sympathetic overactivity with elevated circulating catecholamines, blunted vagal tone, and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis dysregulation, which leaves the myocardium primed for an exaggerated response to an acute stressor. During such an episode, a catecholamine surge acts on apical myocardial beta-receptors and produces a signaling switch from Gs to Gi-mediated pathways, together with microvascular spasm, calcium-handling disturbance, and acute energy failure from supraphysiologic fatty-acid loading; the result is apical akinesis with basal hyperkinesis — the classic takotsubo pattern — in the absence of obstructive coronary disease. The dysfunction resolves in most patients within days to weeks, but a minority have persistent ventricular impairment, and recurrence occurs in a clinically meaningful proportion, which is the basis on which a chronic disability may be claimed. Nayeri et al. (PMID 29544664) reviewed psychiatric illness in takotsubo cardiomyopathy and concluded that there is a strong association between pre-existing psychiatric illness, particularly anxiety and mood spectrum disorders, and takotsubo cardiomyopathy. Lazzeroni et al. (PMID 29168538) compared 58 takotsubo patients with and without pre-existing anxiety disorders and found that a substantial share (31 of 58) had a prior history of anxiety disorders, with the exclusively emotional stressful event rate higher in patients with anxiety disorders. Gonuguntla et al. (PMID 38331372) analyzed the National Inpatient Sample and Nationwide Readmissions Database for 2016 through 2018 and found psychiatric disorders documented in up to 43 percent of takotsubo patients, while examining whether psychiatric comorbidity altered outcomes. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) direct-causation theory, in which the service-connected post-traumatic stress disorder is asserted to have produced a discrete cardiac disease, stress cardiomyopathy, with its own diagnostic code at DC 7020 rather than being folded into the psychiatric evaluation. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory, because the literature describes a new acute cardiac event in a previously unaffected ventricle rather than measurable worsening of an existing structural heart disease; aggravation would govern only where the record documents pre-existing cardiomyopathy or coronary disease and the claim is that the stress-mediated episodes worsened a baseline ventricular dysfunction, in which case the attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of that pre-existing disease and § 3.310(b) applies. Chronology and the individual analysis under § 3.310(a) or (b) require: the diagnosed post-traumatic stress disorder with its documented stressor; an acute coronary syndrome evaluation that excluded obstructive coronary disease; imaging documentation of the characteristic apical ballooning pattern with reduced ejection fraction; a documented emotional or psychological trigger temporally proximate to the episode; and, for a compensable rating, serial echocardiographic evidence of persistent or recurrent left ventricular dysfunction. Only then can an examiner state that the takotsubo cardiomyopathy and any residual dysfunction are at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected post-traumatic stress disorder — a conclusion requiring documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102. Two candid limitations must be disclosed. First, the cited literature concerns psychiatric illness broadly — principally anxiety and mood spectrum disorders — and PTSD-specific data are comparatively limited, so the association cannot be treated as PTSD-specific without individual evidence linking the episodes to PTSD symptoms. Second, takotsubo cardiomyopathy is characteristically transient, so a claim that rests only on a resolved acute episode will fail for lack of residual disability rather than for lack of causation. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include acute coronary syndrome and spontaneous coronary artery dissection, pheochromocytoma and other catecholamine-secreting tumors, sepsis and critical illness, subarachnoid hemorrhage and other acute intracranial events, thyrotoxicosis, cocaine and stimulant use, alcohol withdrawal, perioperative stress, and chemotherapy including fluoropyrimidines and checkpoint inhibitors. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating discipline under § 4.14: a cardiac rating under DC 7020 may not be combined with a second evaluation for the same heart failure symptoms under another heart code, and the psychiatric rating under § 4.130 must not be used to compensate the same limitation of daily functioning that the cardiac evaluation represents.

medicalEvidence.title: Psychiatric Illness in Takotsubo (Stress) Cardiomyopathy: A Review
medicalEvidence.authors: Arash Nayeri; Eric Rafla-Yuan; Srikanth Krishnan; Boback Ziaeian; Martin Cadeiras; John A McPherson; Quinn S Wells
medicalEvidence.summary: Review of psychiatric illness in takotsubo cardiomyopathy concluding that there is a strong association between pre-existing psychiatric illness, particularly anxiety and mood spectrum disorders, and the condition — the principal association evidence for the psychiatric-to-cardiac pathway.

medicalEvidence.title: Anxiety disorders and stressful events in Takotsubo syndrome
medicalEvidence.authors: Davide Lazzeroni; Matteo Bini; Paolo Castiglioni; Luca Moderato; Chiara Ciracì; Umberto Camaiora; Pietro Tito Ugolotti; Lorenzo Brambilla; Valerio Brambilla; Silvia Garibaldi; Letizia Paglialonga; Valentina Ziveri; Luca Brambilla; Daniela Coruzzi; Diego Ardissino; Emilio Giuseppe Ignazio Pela; Paolo Coruzzi
medicalEvidence.summary: Comparative study of 58 takotsubo syndrome patients with and without pre-existing anxiety disorders finding that 31 had a prior history of anxiety disorders and that exclusively emotional triggering events were more frequent in those with anxiety disorders — direct evidence that pre-existing psychological illness shapes the stress-mediated cardiac event.

medicalEvidence.title: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy and psychiatric illness- insight from National Inpatient Sample (NIS) and National Re-admission Database (NRD) 2016 to 2018

medicalEvidence.summary: Analysis of the National Inpatient Sample and Nationwide Readmissions Database for 2016 through 2018 examining outcomes in takotsubo cardiomyopathy patients with and without pre-existing psychiatric disorder and documenting psychiatric comorbidity in a substantial share of takotsubo patients — the large-database confirmation of the psychiatric association.
